item.title: Xi highlights green path to development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Xi highlights green path to development Ecosystem's recovery, computer hub's progress in Inner Mongolia city hailed A first-time visitor looking across the Huangqihai Lake in northern China might find it hard to imagine its dry, exposed lake bed just 20 years ago. When President Xi Jinping visited the lakeside on Friday in Ulaanqab, a city in the Inner Mongolia autonomous region, the water stretched across more than 85 square kilometers. Fish had been detected again in May last year — a sign that the lake's ability to purify itself and sustain aquatic life was gradually recovering. Looking through binoculars at birds on the mudflats, Xi said: "There are quite a few birds. The aquatic ecosystem here has recovered well." The Huangqihai Lake nature reserve was the first stop on a fact-finding trip that also took Xi to the Qahar High-Tech Industrial Development Zone, where the city is expanding its green computing power industry. During the visit, Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, stressed the need to coordinate high-quality development with high-level environmental protection. Fed by 11 rivers, Huangqihai is an inland lake that came close to drying up following decades of drought and other pressures. In recent years, local authorities have dredged waterways feeding the lake, reduced agricultural pollution, restored vegetation and strengthened protection of the reserve. Xi asked whether production activities were still taking place around the lake. Local officials told him that activity in the core area was controlled to reduce human disturbance. He called for giving priority to natural restoration, supplemented by human intervention, in repairing degraded wetland ecosystems. Ban Xiuping, Party secretary of Qahar Right Wing Front Banner, where the lake is located, said local residents have a deep attachment to Huangqihai. Its recovery has helped stabilize agricultural incomes and improve people's living environment, she said. "I think General Secretary Xi's commitment to ecological restoration and conservation is rooted in his deep concern for the people," she said. For Ban, the next milestone would be the return of more fish species. Crucian carp have already been detected, and she hopes common carp and grass carp will follow. Friday's visit was Xi's fourth fact-finding trip to Inner Mongolia since 2012, following trips in 2014, 2019 and 2023. He has repeatedly called for protecting the region's lakes and pursuing the integrated conservation and restoration of mountains, rivers, forests, farmland, lakes, grasslands and deserts. In 2023, he inspected Ulansuhai Nur in Bayannuur and urged sustained efforts to protect it. At Huangqihai, Xi called for sustained efforts to control sand and address overgrazing. He described the region's ecological protection as a national strategy benefiting both Inner Mongolia and the country as a whole. Wu Guoqing, deputy director of Inner Mongolia's forestry and grassland bureau, said the department's work in recent years has included controlling desertification, addressing overgrazing and tackling the destruction of forests and grasslands. According to figures released by the regional forestry and grassland bureau in June, Inner Mongolia's forest coverage has reached 21.98 percent, up 1.19 percentage points from 2021, while grassland vegetation coverage stood at 46.48 percent, its highest level this century. As Ulaanqab works to restore the Huangqihai Lake, it is also developing its computing power industry. Just 240 kilometers from Beijing in a straight line, Ulaanqab offers abundant renewable energy, a climate that allows natural cooling for nearly 10 months a year, and direct fiber-optic links to the capital. At the development zone, Xi learned about Inner Mongolia's progress in building a hub for the "East Data, West Computing" project, a national initiative linking computing power demand in eastern China with resources in western regions. He was also briefed on the development of the city's green computing power industry. Urlug, deputy director of the zone's economic development and investment promotion bureau, said the city's computing power industry has grown in stages. Huawei's arrival in 2013 brought Ulaanqab its first data center. For roughly a decade, the industry focused on storage and general-purpose computing. From 2023 to around the turn of 2026, the city moved into a second phase focused on intelligent computing — the processing capacity used for artificial intelligence — with upgrades to chips, technology and supporting facilities, Urlug said. The third phase, in his description, is closer coordination between computing power and electricity supply. "We are drawing on Ulaanqab's abundant renewable energy resources to develop a green intelligent computing power industry," he said. During the trip, Xi commended the industry's progress and called for extending industrial chains, deepening the integration of the digital and real economies, and translating computing power strengths into development gains. He also examined models of power and cooling systems and asked detailed questions about electricity and water efficiency. Liu Junping, deputy director of the zone's administrative committee, said Xi's attention to water conservation left a strong impression. "In developing computing capacity, we need to plan ahead," Liu said. "Ulaanqab is a water-scarce place. While saving energy, we must also save water." Xi called for efficient, green and safe development, stressing coordination between computing power, electricity supply and water use. He urged those working in the sector to ensure the sound construction and operation of computing centers, actively promote the green computing power industry, and make greater contributions to building Digital China and developing new quality productive forces. His discussions with officials and industry representatives included a warning about the way new industries expand. "What worries me most is disorderly development — everyone rushing in at once and then dispersing all at once, which further dampens enthusiasm," Xi said. He also warned against blind competition and development that disregards local conditions. Urlug said: "Computing power is an emerging industry. We need to get involved early and plan ahead so it develops in an orderly way." The industry is also bringing talented people to Ulaanqab. Zan Deng, manager of the Inner Mongolia Huawang Data Center of Jiangsu Yangdian Science & Technology Co, moved to the city in 2024 to work on the project. More than 70 percent of the company's staff members there have been recruited from elsewhere, she said, with employees settling in the city. Zan was among the industry representatives whom Xi spoke with during the visit. Xi encouraged those present to pursue ambitious goals with patience and determination, describing them as a contingent advancing high-level scientific and technological self-reliance on a new "Long March". "As someone working in this industry, I feel deeply honored and proud to be part of this journey," Zan said. Contact the writers at mojingxi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: US academic retraces Long March
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
US academic retraces Long March William N. Brown shares legacy of Red Army's iconic journey, and vision for global understanding William N. Brown, an American business studies professor at Xiamen University, is celebrating his bond with China that began half a century ago when he served on a United States Air Force base on Taiwan Island in 1976. After leaving the military in 1981, completing his education and selling his business, Brown moved with his family in 1988 to the coastal city of Xiamen in Fujian province. Known for his academic work in business management and promotion of local culture, he in 1992 became the first foreign national in Fujian province to obtain Chinese permanent residency. In 2019, President Xi Jinping congratulated him in a reply letter on the publication of his book, Off the Wall – How We Fell for China. Marking his 50-year bond with the country, the 70-year-old recently embarked on a multimedia project retracing the historic Long March. From October 1934 to October 1936, the Red Army, the precursor to the Chinese People's Liberation Army, marched across treacherous terrain to break the Nationalist Kuomintang regime's encirclement and regroup for the war against Japanese aggression. With some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers while enduring hunger, thirst and cold, the Red Army carried out a daring military maneuver that changed the trajectory of the Communist Party of China and the history of the whole nation. For Brown, however, the journey was deeply visceral. Having previously driven over 200,000 kilometers across every Chinese province — including a grueling 40,000-km road trip in 1994 when he noted road infrastructure was primitive — he still found the physical realities of the Long March staggering. "I could not imagine walking through such terrain, in sweltering heat or freezing winters," Brown said. "Just reading about the Long March is interesting, but it's no more real than watching a historic movie. Even if the facts are correct, you still can't grasp the essence of the joys and sufferings." While retracing the footsteps of the Long March this year, Brown was moved meeting the descendants of those who lost their sons and weren't able to find out where they had died until decades later. "What most impressed me was that even though the Red Army troops, who averaged only 19, I hear, were starving and freezing, and lacked weapons, they never took advantage of the common people," Brown said. Brown found that if the Red Army soldiers received food or clothing, they always found a way to pay for it. "In all of history, I think there was no other 'march' as grueling as this, and yet the soldiers showed their love for China by their love for the people they met. It was not a slogan, 'Love China', but the reality of their love for the people," he said. Later this year, Brown's latest book will be published, entitled Many People, One Dream: Bill Brown's Record of China's Shared Prosperity For All Ethnicities. When revisiting the Long March sites, Brown was especially moved to learn more about how the Red Army treated the Yi ethnic group living near Yihai Lake in Mianning county in Southwest China's Sichuan province. He found that the Yi people initially disliked the Red Army because they thought the Red Army "were just like the Nationalists (led by the Kuomintang regime) and the warlords". "The Red Army could have destroyed the Yi, but instead they very patiently won their trust, helped them understand what they were fighting for — and the Yi made peace with them," Brown said. "This is amazing to me that not just the Han Chinese but the minorities across China supported the Red Army because they all could see clearly that, if the Red Army failed, China would also fall — either to the Japanese or Chiang Kai-shek, or to the warlords or to the foreigners who wanted to divide China into tiny colonies as they did in Africa," he added. In Brown's view, if the Red Army had failed to reach Yan'an, which is located in today's Shaanxi province and was home to a revolutionary base, "Japan would likely have conquered China, and then the rest of Asia". "History is like a lot of little dominos falling, and something that seems insignificant now might loom much larger months or years later. So in telling the Long March story, I think it's important to help foreigners see what was really at stake," he said.

item.title: AI expands access to traditional medicine
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
AI expands access to traditional medicine Artificial intelligence is now being widely applied to enhance traditional medicine, making it more accessible, standardized and research-based, according to a report released on Sunday on the sidelines of the 2026 World Conference on Traditional Medicine in Beijing. Centuries-old traditional remedies have typically relied on wisdom passed down through a teacher-disciple tradition, and often lack the scientific rigor and diagnostic standards adopted by modern medicine. Li Haiyan, director of the Institute of Information on Traditional Chinese Medicine of the China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences, which led the report, said that AI tools can turn accumulated practices into knowledge and data that can be stored, programmed and validated. She was speaking at the launch of the report examining AI's applications in the global development of traditional medicine. The report was initiated by the Global Alliance for Traditional and Integrative Medicine and was released during the 2026 World Conference on Traditional Medicine, which was held over the weekend. Premier Li Qiang also underlined the need to harness science and technology to accelerate the innovative development of traditional medicine. While addressing the opening ceremony of the conference on Saturday, he said China will promote the digital and intelligent transformation of TCM and encourage and support active participation of Chinese and foreign research institutions and enterprises. The report said that AI-empowered traditional medicine has entered a phase of rapid development, as a number of nations have incorporated the technology into broader health development strategies. In a sign of evolving technologies, a total of 3,030 AI-related traditional medicine patents have been published globally since 2000, and 6,882 high-quality academic papers have been released since 1990, the report said. China accounted for 80.4 percent of the patents and 47 percent of the academic papers, demonstrating the scale of the nation's research and technological advantage in this field, it added. In clinical practice, Li, the researcher, said that AI has been used to assist in examinations of a patient's tongue, pulse, facial appearance and other aspects, as well as in diagnosis. For some syndromes, AI-assisted tongue diagnosis has proved to be 85 to 92 percent accurate, with the ability to distinguish experience-based symptom descriptions such as "a reddish tongue". "Some digital twin models trained on the clinical experience, diagnostic reasoning and typical case records of renowned TCM practitioners have already been piloted in China's county-level TCM hospitals to expand access to quality TCM resources," she said. AI has also been used to digitalize the surveying, identification, cultivation and supply chain traceability of medicinal plants, accelerate the screening of active ingredients and analysis of drug mechanisms, and advance basic research in areas such as jing luo, also known as meridians, through which the body's energy is believed to circulate. Moreover, Li said AI has enabled more systematic reviews of ancient medical texts to bolster innovative inheritance of traditional practices. In one case cited in the report, researchers used deep learning-assisted in vivo imaging to observe dynamic changes in immune cells in mouse models after electroacupuncture stimulation, offering a new perspective on how acupuncture points regulate the immune system, said Chen Jianxin, a professor at Beijing University of Chinese Medicine. In addition to TCM, Chen said the report showcases AI-powered inheritance among traditional Korean medicine practitioners, as well as smart diagnostic devices for Ayurveda, the traditional system of medicine originating in India. Chen said the uneven development of digital capabilities globally has affected traditional medicine's adoption of AI. More efforts are needed to accumulate high-quality datasets, address language differences between countries as well as between ancient and modern times, provide clearer explanations of medical mechanisms, and promote the establishment of unified supervision regulations targeting AI-assisted traditional medicine, he added. wangxiaoyu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Folk dance moves become surprise online hit
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
A sudden twist, a swift shift of weight, a vigorous shake of the shoulders — moves once taught in a Beijing dance classroom nearly a decade ago have become the latest social media sensations, inspiring millions to give Chinese folk dance a try. Two moves, dubbed "Shanshen Step" and "Bear Shaking off Its Fur" by Chinese internet users, have become unlikely viral hits, inspiring imitations, comic remakes and online challenges. Some users have joked that mastering the "Shanshen Step" could help them squeeze into a packed rush-hour subway train, while others have turned the moves into playful routines that mock the idea of sneaking away from work. The trend has also taken on a life of its own, with people adding their own twists and even artificial intelligence-generated characters to add to the fun. But these seemingly quirky moves are no internet inventions — both originate from traditional Chinese folk dance moves and were filmed years ago as part of the Beijing Dance Academy's teaching material. The demonstrators, Zhao Tiechun and Ming Wenjun, are respected veterans of China's dance community. Now, the clips are being seen well beyond China. As the United States-based Martha Graham Dance Company prepares to perform in the country in November, principal dancers Xin Ying and Lloyd Knight have joined the trend, showing off their own versions of the moves. German fitness influencer Pamela Reif has also filmed herself trying the "Shanshen Step". The unexpected popularity of the moves has brought fresh attention to Chinese folk dance. Tian Lu, a professor at the Beijing Dance Academy who participated in the original recordings, said the "Shanshen Step" comes from Anhui Huagudeng, a traditional folk dance in Anhui province. The move involves a sudden move of the body and a change of direction. In folk performance, it is part of a continuous sequence of movements. The exercise allows practitioners to work on shifting their center of gravity quickly and initiating movement through a controlled tilt of the body. The other viral move, "Bear Shaking off Its Fur", comes from Shandong Guzi Yangge, a traditional folk dance in Shandong province. Traditionally performed mainly by men, the dance features vigorous movements and rhythmic patterns, with drums among its signature props. The teaching videos were designed to break down the cultural and physical elements of folk dance into exercises that university students could study and practice. The team did not expect the clips to become internet sensations years later. For Tian, however, the movements' appeal is not entirely surprising. "Folk dancers move naturally, without rigid rules," she said. Expansive movements can express powerful emotions, while restrained gestures convey subtler feelings. The movements grow out of authentic expression and the humor found in Chinese folk culture, she added. The craze has even spilled onto the stage. Dye House (Da Ran Fang), a dance drama directed and choreographed by Guo Haifeng and produced by the Shandong Song and Dance Theater, incorporates the "Bear Shaking off Its Fur" movement. The production premiered in April and is touring nationwide, with the viral attention generating new curiosity about the work. Guo, who was also trained at the Beijing Dance Academy, sees the online craze as an unexpected opportunity to reconnect audiences with the art form. The movements have always belonged to a world beyond the studio, Guo added. "They come from everyday life, become teaching material and eventually return to the people," he said. "Now everyone is learning them. Art comes from life, returns to life and becomes part of life. If people like something, they will imitate it. That is a good thing." Zhao, who demonstrated the "Shanshen Step", likewise sees the viral success as both surprising and understandable. "It was unexpected, but in a way, it was also to be expected," he said. "The knowledge embedded in Chinese folk dance needs to be passed down. These teaching videos meet the needs of teachers and students, while also helping preserve the culture itself." The "Shanshen Step", he said, combines the distinctive features of traditional folk culture with qualities that make it easy to share and adapt online. Zhao sees the trend as an example of a new form of popular cultural expression, created by the audience. "People are taking movements from Chinese folk dance and turning them into something that speaks to their own feelings and sense of fun today," he said. "They recognize the movements, try them out and put their own spin on them. If it makes people happy and sparks new ideas, that is what makes it interesting." However, there is one important caveat. Experts cited by CCTV News warned that imitating the moves without proper training can put the knees at risk.

item.title: Journalists' role in BRI cooperation highlighted
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Journalists' role in BRI cooperation highlighted Journalists play a crucial role in building the Belt and Road and advancing international cooperation on global governance, as they bridge nations, cultures and communities, media leaders said at the 2026 Belt and Road Journalists Forum held on Saturday in Nanjing, Jiangsu province. Themed "Convergence and Connectivity · Innovation and Progress · Media Transformation amid Global Changes", the forum gathered nearly 100 journalists and media leaders from over 50 countries and regions. Mo Gaoyi, deputy head of the Publicity Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and director of the State Council Information Office, noted in his remarks that the Belt and Road Journalists Network has made significant contributions toward advancing the high-quality joint construction of the Belt and Road. Mo noted that the world is undergoing unprecedented changes, and global media cooperation is becoming increasingly critical for strengthening connectivity between people, infrastructure, rules and standards. He added that China's journalist community hopes to strengthen international communication, telling Belt and Road stories together through objective and truthful reporting that showcases the diversity of civilizations coexisting in harmony. Mo also stressed the need to deepen practical cooperation on media transformation in the era of artificial intelligence, and to promote coordination with Global South nations so that their stories are better heard on the global stage. John Wallace, executive director of the Asia Pacific Journalism Centre, said that in this rapidly changing world, better communication and trust are essential, in order to overcome prejudice, ignorance and misunderstanding. They are also vital both for preventing unnecessary conflict today and building a more effective and inclusive system of global governance in the future. "Journalism has a crucial role to play because it shapes how nations perceive one another. One of its greatest challenges is to understand and accurately convey the profound changes that have taken place across Asia and other developing regions in recent decades," said Wallace. He Ping, president of the All-China Journalists Association and a member of the presidium of the Belt and Road Journalists Network, pointed out that, faced with rising unilateralism and protectionism, the global community is in greater need of upholding the Silk Road spirit of peace and cooperation, openness and inclusiveness, mutual learning and mutual benefit. With pens and cameras, He called for closer ties among global journalists to bridge different civilizations and people, contributing to the world's stability and vitality. Chroniclers, promoters Participants at the forum agreed that journalists are the chroniclers, participants and promoters in jointly building the Belt and Road, which has now entered a new phase of development characterized by higher quality and higher standards. They also reached consensus that media communities across nations should share Belt and Road stories through objective and truthful reporting, with a focus on major landmark projects as well as smaller, heartwarming life stories. "Global cooperation requires more than physical infrastructure, trade and economic partnerships. It also requires communication, cultural exchange and mutual trust. As journalists, we can build bridges between nations by sharing reliable information, respecting cultural differences and encouraging dialogue," said Puy Kea, president of the Club of Cambodian Journalists and rotating president of the presidium of the Belt and Road Journalists Network. He added that despite differences in their nationalities, cultures and political systems, journalists and media leaders are not merely observers of global change, but also help shape public understanding, promote transparency and bring the voices of diverse communities to the international stage. "The 'Silk Road spirit' is about learning together and growing together," said Zuzana Lechanova, a news reporter with Slovak Television. "Each of our countries has a different system, culture and traditions. But what connects us is our search for truth and our fight against prejudice. If we want people to support the Belt and Road Initiative, we must tell them true stories — stories about our success, but also about our challenges." wangxin2@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: AI brewing fresh global growth for Chinese tech
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
AI brewing fresh global growth for Chinese tech Homegrown products gaining popularity, with GBA players leading in intelligent hardware Amid the sleek consumer gadgets on display at IFA 2026 in Berlin, Germany, a Chinese-made heavy-duty quadruped robot offered a glimpse into a broader shift in China's artificial intelligence sector — homegrown technologies are moving beyond laboratories and consumer devices into demanding real-world operations. The Hypertron-T01, developed by Shenzhen-based Astrall Dynamics, is designed to carry heavy loads and navigate steep slopes, gravel and slippery surfaces, capabilities aimed at power inspections, emergency response and other environments where reliability matters as much as intelligence. It was named a winner in the Best in IFA Next & Emerging Technologies category at the IFA 2026 Innovation Awards. The robot's appearance at the IFA reflects how Chinese AI hardware companies are building a new competitive edge around proprietary technologies, engineering execution and the ability to turn algorithms into products that can withstand continuous industrial use, rather than relying mainly on cost advantages. "The robot effectively addresses challenges in specialized industrial scenarios such as power inspections, campus security and emergency firefighting, where both speed and stability under heavy loads are required," said Lin Shenchu, head of marketing at Astrall Dynamics. That progress is increasingly being tested in operating environments at home before reaching markets overseas. Hypertron-series robots, for example, have undergone long-term unmanned operations in substations run by leading Chinese power grid companies, generating data and experience for further product refinements. According to the company, its self-developed power system enables the Hypertron-T01 to carry a maximum dynamic load of 80 kilograms while limiting overheating and performance degradation under heavy loads. Such advances point to a wider transition in China's AI sector from showcasing stand-alone technologies to delivering scalable systems and solutions for industrial needs around the world. The company's strategy for international expansion involves not only selling products, but also working with local partners to co-develop industry-specific applications, Lin said, adding that the company, established in 2024, plans to open core software development kit (SDK) interfaces covering motion control, sensor data and device management to partners in Europe. "The move is intended to shorten the development cycle for industry-specific solutions from six months to a few months by collaborating with global integrators, solution providers and developers to expand the range of industrial applications," said Lin, adding that opening the SDK interfaces will enable local European partners to develop solutions tailored to specific operating environments more quickly. "These solutions can go global because they address challenges facing industries worldwide, including severe labor shortages and aging populations, as well as growing staffing gaps in high-risk jobs, night-shift inspections and repetitive tasks." The trend was also visible at IFA 2026 as embodied AI moved from screens into the physical world. More than 1,000 exhibitors from the Chinese mainland and Hong Kong participated in the event, marking a record level of Chinese participation. During IFA 2026, which was held in early September, Chinese exhibitors showcased their strengths in AI applications, supply chain management, engineering execution and ecosystem collaboration, demonstrating capabilities essential to the large-scale deployment of AI.

item.title: Canada looks to China to diversify trade
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Canada looks to China as trade diversification gains momentum Ottawa building economy less vulnerable to pressure from Washington, experts say Canada is stepping up efforts to diversify its trade as a renewed tariff confrontation with the United States puts fresh pressure on Ottawa to broaden its economic relationships. The US imposed a 50 percent tariff on C$27.6 billion ($19.6 billion) worth of Canadian goods effective Aug 22, prompting Canada to impose matching counter-tariffs on selected US products from Sept 8. The Canadian government has since emphasized the need to diversify trade and reduce dependence on any single partner. On Sept 29, a US ban on nearly $1 billion in annual imports from Canada took effect, targeting most Canadian alcoholic beverages, some dairy products and certain motorcycles. US President Donald Trump recently described Canada as "very difficult to deal with" and said: "Canada would like to make a deal, but we're not satisfied with it." Ron Stagg, a professor of history at Toronto Metropolitan University who studies Canadian-American relations, said the Canadian response to the latest US tariffs was being driven not only by economic considerations but also by growing frustration with what Ottawa sees as continuing demands from Washington. "Up until now the Carney government has treated the American government as a tough negotiator that will respond to conciliatory steps," Stagg told China Daily. "However, it is clear now that every time Canada gives a little, the US makes new demands," he said. He said the trade confrontation would reinforce Canada's efforts to build an economy that was less vulnerable to US pressure. China has emerged as one of the most significant destinations in that effort, with bilateral trade showing stronger export momentum in the first half of this year and both governments moving to restore market access in several areas. Canadian exports to China rose 30.1 percent year-on-year to C$21.74 billion in the first half of 2026, while imports from China fell 5.8 percent to C$44.86 billion, according to a report released by the Canada China Business Council and the China Institute at the University of Alberta. Total merchandise trade reached C$66.6 billion, up 3.6 percent from a year earlier. Bijan Ahmadi, executive director and COO of the Canada China Business Council, told China Daily the "most significant takeaway from the first half of 2026 is that Canada-China trade became more export-oriented". But the change in imports does not necessarily point to a broad retreat from Chinese products, he said. "The import decline was not a uniform retreat from Chinese supply: consumer goods and electronics weakened, while machinery, batteries and vehicles continued to grow," Ahmadi said, adding that full-year data would be needed before drawing broader conclusions. The report described the relationship as expanding "selectively rather than uniformly".

item.title: Young docents keep Long March story alive in Sichuan
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Young docents keep Long March story alive in Sichuan In May 1935, Liu Bocheng, a Red Army commander, and Xiao Yedan, head of the Guoji clan of the Yi ethnic group, swore a blood oath by the Yihai Lake in Mianning county, Liangshan Yi autonomous prefecture, Sichuan province. The alliance enabled the Red Army to pass through Yi-inhabited areas and bought it time for the subsequent forced crossing of the Dadu River and the swift capture of the Luding Bridge during the Long March. More than 90 years later, young "Red Scarf" docents in Mianning are keeping the story alive. Moved by the story, one visitor said, "This must be told to more people." Since last year, more than 80 primary school students have taken part in docent training. While the storytellers change, ethnic unity and mutual support remain unchanged.

item.title: What stands out in China's sustainable development?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
World Bank director Tatiana Rosito: In sustainable development, what stands out in China's experience? What stands out in China's experience of sustainable development? In a recent interview with China Daily's Global Lens, Tatiana Rosito, World Bank director for China, Mongolia and Korea, said China has "interesting, scalable and replicable" experience in its development, worth sharing with the world. She first affirms China's ecosystem restoration, adding that the Bank and China have worked together on fighting desertification and preventing erosion for more than 20 years. Then environmental solutions: China's experience in controlling air and water pollution is a ready-made example. And the rural-urban link — building sustainable, livable cities and a circular economy — is, she says, exactly the area developing partners most want to work on with China. Under the dual-carbon goals, the energy transition is likewise a good topic for knowledge cooperation. The "knowledge agenda" she describes runs both ways: inward, to help fill China's gaps; outward, using the World Bank's global reach and analytical skills to curate and translate Chinese solutions so other countries can adapt them to local conditions. In the next five years, she expects the World Bank to continue walking alongside China on sustainable development. (Reporter: Li Wei, Video: Pan Yixuan and Cheng Zixin)
